generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport this shows up in the habits each subject lives by. Which questions count as empirical, how evidence from a physiology test or a field study is weighed, and how practical and ethical limits shape what you may even ask: these differ across the school. A sport scientist trusts lab data and control; a coach trusts what a session reveals; a management student trusts participation figures. Early on much of this is unspoken, picked up from how your lecturers reason about studies and what your reading treats as sound method. Noticing those habits, and trying them in your own lab reports and seminar arguments, is how you start to take part in sport as a discipline rather than just revise it.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two sport and exercise science students preparing for the same seminar on the same physiology study.

Tom reads the study once and highlights the findings, ready to repeat them if asked. The VO2 max results are in his notes and the paper has been covered. This is surface learning: the information has been taken in, but it sits on its own, and he treats the study as a set of numbers to recall.

Amara reads the same study and keeps asking why. Why did the authors choose this testing protocol? How does the small, trained sample limit what the findings can claim? Where would a different model of fatigue predict something else? By the seminar, Amara can connect the study to a wider debate about method and evidence in exercise physiology, and take a reasoned position within it. This is deep learning: the ideas are linked into understanding she can use and defend.

Both students have read the study. Only Amara has taken the step the sport-science community values, turning reported findings into a judgement about how good the evidence is.
generatedProse.summary: Learning in the School of Sport means joining a discourse community that makes, tests and argues about evidence together, ethically and by shared methods. You can now identify what makes that different from recalling findings, and begin to recognise the community your own sport subject draws on, whether that is exercise physiology, coaching or management. The move from surface to deep learning, and the habits that support it, will matter in every lesson that follows and in your first lab report or practical write-up.

check.body: Which of these would best help you recognise the discourse community of your subject in the School of Sport?

items.text: Noticing who produces and debates the key studies and practice, and how they argue from evidence and method.
Counting how many studies your textbook cites, and tallying which topics come up the most often.
Learning the timetable for your lab and practical sessions, and working out which rooms they run in.
Memorising the names of the researchers, and the years their best-known studies were published.

feedback.correct: That's right. You recognise a sport subject's discourse community by seeing who makes its knowledge and how they reason from evidence and method, not by counting studies or learning logistics.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about how knowledge is made and argued from evidence, rather than counts or logistics.
feedback.incorrectFinal: You recognise the discourse community of a sport subject by noticing who produces and debates its key studies and practice, and how they argue from evidence and method. The other options are about quantity or logistics, not how the community makes knowledge.
